questions.question: What is a goroutine and how is it different from an OS thread?
questions.title: Goroutines vs threads
questions.direct_answer: A goroutine is a lightweight concurrent function managed by the Go runtime. The runtime multiplexes many goroutines over a smaller pool of OS threads, so they start cheaply, but shared data still needs synchronization.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming goroutines remove data races or always make code faster.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention structured cancellation with context and a wait mechanism such as sync.WaitGroup.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Goroutines vs threads simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Lightweight concurrency
sections.content: Starting a goroutine with go schedules a function independently. Channels can coordinate ownership of values; mutexes protect shared state when sharing is intentional.

sections.title: Wait for work
sections.content:
```go
var wg sync.WaitGroup
wg.Add(1)
go func() { defer wg.Done(); work() }()
wg.Wait()
```

sections.title: Remember
items: Goroutines are runtime-managed, not free of scheduling cost.
Use channels or synchronization to coordinate.
Always define how goroutines stop to avoid leaks.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A goroutine is a lightweight function scheduled by the Go runtime across OS threads. It makes concurrency inexpensive, but I still design ownership, cancellation, and synchronization explicitly because goroutines do not prevent races by themselves.

sections.title: Concept explained
sections.content: Walk through the example step by step, then say when this approach is a good fit and what you would test at the boundary.
